The first time I tried to repair a chair, I made it shorter. One leg wobbled, so I sanded it. Then the opposite leg wobbled, which seemed unfair, since it had been perfectly well behaved a minute earlier. By lunchtime the chair stood level, but anyone sitting in it looked like a child waiting for a haircut.

My neighbor Ruth found me measuring the kitchen table, considering a corresponding adjustment. She brought over a scrap of cork and showed me how to glue it beneath the original offending leg. “You can add things, too,” she said.

I keep that sentence handy. When a paragraph drags, I tend to cut it. Sometimes what it needs is one good detail: the wet cuff, the bus ticket gone soft in somebody’s palm. When a friend grows quiet, I start editing my last conversation, looking for the remark I ought to take back. Sometimes I just need to bring soup.

The chair now lives by the front door. Its reduced height makes it exactly right for putting on boots. Ruth sits there after our Sunday walks, unlacing hers slowly because her fingers hurt in cold weather. I put the kettle on. We rarely discuss the chair, except when a visitor compliments it, in which case Ruth says it was made to measure.

She is technically right. I measured that thing eleven times. What I never thought to measure was the distance from a tired person’s hand to the knot in a muddy lace. Now I know.
